clue.text: Stuffed shirt for one of 550 opening present from GI up

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the built word is read from bottom to top
the pieces go into the opening of the word for present, splitting it

parts.note: an American soldier answers a roll call with Yo, meaning here or present
eg, for example, means for one
DL is 550 in Roman numerals (D 500, L 50)

explanation.surface: A pompous person, a sample of 550, opens a gift sent by an American soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift, but it is a soldier's answer to a roll call, YO. YO round EGOFDL, read upwards, gives OLDFOGEY.
explanation.definitionFit: A stuffed shirt is a pompous, conventional person, as an old fogey is: stuffy and behind the times.

clue.text: Doctor snubbed sweet food to save vital missing energy

indicators.note: saving something means keeping it safe within, so one piece is held inside

parts.note: JELLY, a sweet dessert, with its tail cut short

indicators.note: snub means cut short, as with a snub nose, so the last letter is cut off
whatever is missing is left out of the word before it

parts.note: key means vital, essential
E is the physics symbol for energy; it is the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Someone shortchanged on a pudding is told to keep back something essential that has run out of steam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' here means truncated, as in a snub nose, not insulted; and 'missing energy' applies to the vital word alone, before it goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Dr Jekyll is the respectable physician in Stevenson's novella who turns into Mr Hyde.

clue.text: Tribe given lift united during pilgrimage

indicators.note: in a down answer, being lifted up means the letters are read bottom to top
something that happens during an event sits within it

parts.note: the hadj, also spelt hajj, is the Muslim pilgrimage to Mecca
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A tribe on pilgrimage is given a ride and travels together.
explanation.walkthrough: U goes inside HADJ to make HADUJ, which reads upwards in the grid. HADJ is one accepted spelling of hajj.
explanation.definitionFit: Judah is one of the twelve tribes of Israel, descended from Jacob's son of that name.

clue.text: Florida Keys residents grasping I work for hospital porters

indicators.note: grasping means the residents' word holds the new letters inside it
for means one thing stands in place of another, here the letters replace hospital

parts.note: Conchs (or Conches) is the nickname for people born in the Florida Keys
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
the erg is the physics unit of work

explanation.surface: Residents of the Florida Keys taking on work as hospital porters.
explanation.walkthrough: Conchs is the name for natives of the Florida Keys, from the shellfish; take CONCHES, and put I and ERG in place of its H.
explanation.definitionFit: Concierges are hotel or apartment porters who look after doors and guests' needs.

clue.text: Radio's top dog

indicators.note: on the radio we only hear words, so what counts is the sound, not the spelling

parts.note: the top of a mountain is its peak

explanation.surface: A boast that some broadcaster is the leading star of the airwaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' looks like one phrase for a boss; it splits into the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Peke is the short informal name for a Pekingese, a small long-haired breed originally from China.

clue.text: Folk didn't believe her Señor's limits within his own house

indicators.note: whatever is within something else is placed inside it

parts.note: casa is Spanish for house, the language the señor would use
the first and last letters of Señor are S and R, written out in full as S AND R

explanation.surface: A woman nobody trusted is shut up within the walls of a Spanish gentleman's home.
explanation.walkthrough: The limits of Señor are 'S and R', and that whole phrase, AND included, goes inside CASA; 'his own' points to Spanish.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Cassandra, a Trojan princess, was cursed to prophesy truly but never be believed by anyone.

clue.text: Opinionated men sadly won't have it, one attitude primarily

definitions.text: Opinionated men sadly won't have it, one attitude primarily

indicators.note: sadly signals that the letters of the first words are in a bad state, jumbled
won't have means these letters must be left out of the jumble
primarily means only the first letter of attitude is taken

parts.note: its first letter is used

explanation.surface: A wry complaint that dogmatic men never take on a receptive outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the letters of OPINIONATED MEN, remove those of IT, ONE and A (the first letter of attitude), and rearrange what remains; the whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being receptive to new ideas is exactly the attitude that the opinionated lack, so the whole clue defines it.

clue.text: A little wound felt tender — it stings

indicators.note: wound as in wound back, like a tape rewound, so the letters run backwards
only a little of the phrase is used, a run of letters lying inside it

parts.note: the run of letters inside these two words, before being turned round

explanation.surface: A small cut felt sore, because a plant stung it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wound' reads as an injury, which fits the stinging; here it is the past tense of wind.
explanation.definitionFit: The common nettle is a weed whose leaves carry tiny hairs that inject an irritant on touch.

clue.text: After withdrawal of meat, you finally reduce sugar

indicators.note: withdrawing means drawing back, so the letters are pulled back the other way

parts.note: veal is calf meat

indicators.note: finally points at the very end, so just the last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of you
as in to lose weight

explanation.surface: Advice to a dieter: once you've given up meat, cut back on the sugar too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduce' works in the slimming sense, as in to lose weight; laevulose is the older British spelling of levulose.
explanation.definitionFit: Laevulose is another name for fructose, the simple fruit sugar that rotates polarised light leftward.

clue.text: Primate outside public library forbidden fruit

indicators.note: one thing outside another wraps around it

parts.note: an ape is a primate
PL is the abbreviation for public library

explanation.surface: A monkey loiters outside the public library with something it is not allowed to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The fruit Eve took in Eden is traditionally pictured as an apple, though Genesis never names it. The apple also ties to the oak apple of the puzzle's theme.
explanation.definitionFit: Popular tradition makes the fruit of the tree of knowledge an apple, so it is the classic forbidden fruit.

clue.text: Tom's children disturbing promotional material: some of them spotted?

indicators.note: something disturbing a group barges into the middle of it

parts.note: flyers are advertising leaflets
a tom is a male cat
CH is the abbreviation for children

explanation.surface: A cat's kittens scatter a pile of leaflets, some of which turn out to be stained.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spotted' hints at the spotted flycatcher, a common bird; the question mark flags the definition as a hint by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Flycatchers are small birds that catch insects in flight, and the spotted flycatcher is one well-known species.

clue.text: Head teachers, now retired

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an informal word for the skull
second meaning: the initials of a former British teaching union

explanation.surface: A former headmaster and his colleagues have all left the profession.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Union of Teachers merged into the National Education Union in 2017, hence 'now retired'.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang uses this word for the head, and it was the abbreviation of a British trade union for teachers.

clue.text: Sore neck

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a sore rubbed on the skin, as on a horse
second meaning: neck as in cheek, impudence

explanation.walkthrough: Read together it is a stiff neck; 'neck' is the slang for nerve or effrontery. An oak apple is a gall, tying to the 29 May theme.
explanation.definitionFit: A gall is a chafed sore on the skin, and gall also means brazen impudence, the same as neck or cheek.

clue.text: Misguidedly agree with one about part of flying machine

indicators.note: something misguided is going the wrong way, so the letters are set in a wrong order
about suggests turning things round and round, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
with in the sense of using, as in written in ink
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone foolishly assents to a colleague's view about a component of an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is AGREE + IN + ONE, ten letters shuffled together.
explanation.definitionFit: An aero-engine is the power unit of an aircraft, one component of the whole machine.

clue.text: Not upright, Telegraph's concealing refusal to admit fall in circulation

indicators.note: concealing means the newspaper's word wraps round the rest

parts.note: the setter writes for the Telegraph, so the paper's possession is ours

indicators.note: to admit means the refusal takes the next letters inside it

parts.note: no is a refusal

indicators.note: in circulation means the letters go round, the front letter moving to the back

parts.note: the word is used as written before being rotated

explanation.surface: The Telegraph is said to be hiding a refusal to admit its readership is falling.
explanation.walkthrough: The Telegraph's setter calls the paper ours. 'In circulation' rotates fall to ALLF, which NO is made 'to admit', giving NALLFO for OURS to be 'concealing'.
explanation.definitionFit: On all fours means crawling on hands and knees, so the body is not standing upright.

clue.text: Supernumerary bishop in upstairs WC is in charge

indicators.note: a thing in another is placed inside it

parts.note: a mine is an explosive charge; it holds the rest

indicators.note: in a down answer, upstairs means climbing, so the letters read bottom to top
something that is in another sits inside it

parts.note: a loo is a WC, a toilet
RR, Right Reverend, is a bishop's title

explanation.surface: An extra cleric is installed in the upstairs lavatory and put in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests responsibility, which 'in charge' reinforces; it is an explosive. Right Reverend is the formal style of an Anglican bishop.
explanation.definitionFit: A supernumerary is an extra actor with no lines, someone who plays only a small part on stage.

clue.text: With a wrench vote against revolutionary leader

indicators.note: a revolution is a turn right round, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: nay is a vote against
a king is a leader

explanation.surface: A wrenching, violent vote against a rebel chief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary leader' wants to be one figure, like Lenin; 'revolutionary' instead turns the vote round. The king links to Charles II's restoration.
explanation.definitionFit: Yanking is pulling hard with a sudden jerk, which is doing something with a wrench.

clue.text: Source of oranges large Cornish town imports after sending whiskey south

indicators.note: imports means the town takes the letters inside it
south in a down clue means further down the word, where the whiskey letter is put back
sending the whiskey letter away means it is lifted out of its place in the town

parts.note: Newlyn is a fishing town in Cornwall, in south-west England
W is whiskey in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Cornish town importing large quantities of oranges, with whiskey shipped south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After sending whiskey south' moves the town's W further down: lifted out it leaves NELYN, which 'imports' LG with the W after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Nell Gwyn was famous as an orange-seller at Drury Lane theatre before becoming Charles II's mistress.

clue.text: Diversion for two pairs in pursuit of a contract

indicators.note: one thing in pursuit of another follows behind it, so it comes second

parts.note: taken as written
bridge is a card game for four players in two partnerships

explanation.surface: A card game where two partnerships chase a contract, which in bridge is the bid to be made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a bridge term, which fits the surface; it is a verb meaning shorten.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten or condense it, making it contract in length.

clue.text: Maybe Jersey, former monarch's location to the north, where king's ghost walks?

indicators.note: in a down answer, heading north means upward, so the letters read bottom to top

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen's cipher
on is a preposition of location, as in on the table
Jersey is an example of an island

explanation.surface: A spooky tale: on Jersey, north of where an old monarch once stayed, a royal phantom stalks.
explanation.walkthrough: ER + ON + ISLE reads upwards. Jersey is one of the Channel Islands, off France.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is set at Elsinore castle in Denmark, where the ghost of Hamlet's murdered father walks the battlements.

clue.text: Deed from lawyer, turning out to be so fallible

indicators.note: turning something out empties and jumbles it, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A legal document drawn up by a solicitor proves to be riddled with errors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning out to be' reads as one phrase; 'turning out' is the anagram signal and 'to be' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill of sale is a formal legal document transferring ownership of goods from seller to buyer.

clue.text: Second-class PM in brief conflict

parts.note: B is a second-class grade

indicators.note: brief means cut short, the last letter dropped

parts.note: Clement Attlee was British Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951

explanation.surface: A second-rate prime minister caught up briefly in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Attlee was the Labour Prime Minister after the Second World War; his name is cut short and follows B.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle is a fight between armed forces, a conflict.

clue.text: Letters restaurant's clientele delivered

indicators.note: a speech is delivered out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: the customers of a restaurant are diners

explanation.surface: Mail addressed to the customers of a restaurant has arrived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Letters ... delivered' suggests post; the letters are Greek ones, and 'delivered' signals speech. In non-rhotic British speech the two words sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet, so etas are letters of that alphabet.

clue.text: A few dry leaves first to shrivel

indicators.note: when something leaves, it goes away, so that letter is taken out

parts.note: thirsty means dry, wanting a drink

indicators.note: the first to do something is the one at the front, so only the opening letter counts

parts.note: the first letter of shrivel; taken away

explanation.surface: A handful of withered leaves are the first to curl up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' is the verb, not foliage, which the dry, shrivelling surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Thirty is a modest number, so in a loose sense it amounts to a few of something.

clue.text: "Monotonous" perhaps encapsulates the compiler

indicators.note: to encapsulate is to enclose in a capsule, so one piece holds another

parts.note: say means perhaps, for example
the setter refers to themselves

explanation.surface: A sly self-deprecating line: the setter admits his style might be called monotonous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The compiler' is the setter speaking of themselves, so it gives ME; 'perhaps' is SAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Samey is informal for repetitive and unvaried, so something samey is dull and monotonous.

clue.text: Day of the German game

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the German word for day
second meaning: the chasing game children play

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a German team's match day; 'of the German' means in the German language.
explanation.definitionFit: Tag is German for day, and also the playground chasing game where whoever is 'it' touches another.

clue.text: Making good speech following a snooze?

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so this piece goes second

parts.note: a snooze is a rest
an oration is a formal speech

explanation.surface: An after-dinner speaker who perks up after a nap.
explanation.walkthrough: The Restoration of Charles II in 1660 is the event Oak Apple Day, 29 May, commemorates.
explanation.definitionFit: Restoration is the act of repairing or renewing something, which is what making good means.

clue.text: Cut it with knight

parts.note: it means sex appeal, abbreviated SA
W is the abbreviation for with
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut something with a knight, as if wielding his sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' in the old slang sense is sex appeal, which crosswords abbreviate to SA.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawn is the past participle of saw, so something sawn has been cut through.

clue.text: True of the king, changing sides

indicators.note: changing sides means swapping right for left, so R becomes L

parts.note: royal means belonging to the king

explanation.surface: A courtier's oath that something belongs to the king and yet has defected.
explanation.walkthrough: R and L are the abbreviations for right and left; switching the side turns royal into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Loyal means faithful and steadfast, as a true friend is.

clue.text: City brawl about secret bonkers

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the letters face the other way

parts.note: a row is a noisy quarrel

indicators.note: bonkers means crazy, so the letters go wildly out of order

parts.note: taken as written, as the fodder

explanation.surface: A town-centre fight breaks out over some secret that is utterly mad.
explanation.walkthrough: ROW is the quarrel sense (rhyming with cow). Worcester is the battle of 1651 after which Charles II hid in an oak tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Worcester is a cathedral city in the English West Midlands, on the River Severn.
